train.content: what is the OWASP Top 10?

OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web security vulnerabilities. 1) Broken Access Control: unauthorized access like normal users reaching admin pages. 2) Cryptographic Failures: sensitive data unencrypted, sending passwords over HTTP. 3) Injection: SQL, NoSQL, OS command injection. 4) Insecure Design: security not considered during design phase. 5) Security Misconfiguration: default passwords, unnecessary services exposed. 6) Vulnerable Components: outdated libraries with known vulnerabilities. 7) Authentication Failures: weak identity verification. 8) Software/Data Integrity Failures: updates from untrusted sources. 9) Logging & Monitoring Failures: attacks go undetected. 10) SSRF: Server-Side Request Forgery. Every web developer should know this list and verify their projects against it.

train.content: how do you design a CI/CD pipeline?

CI/CD is continuous integration and continuous deployment — automatically testing and deploying code changes. A good pipeline: 1) Automatically triggered on code push (GitHub webhook). 2) Lint and format checks. 3) Unit tests run. 4) Integration tests. 5) Docker image is built. 6) Deploy to staging environment. 7) E2E tests run on staging. 8) Manual approval for production. 9) Production deploy. Tools: GitHub Actions (free, easy), GitLab CI, Jenkins (self-hosted, flexible), CircleCI. Best practices: keep the pipeline fast (under 10 minutes ideal), run tests in parallel, use caching, fail fast (catch errors early). For Gorkem's projects, GitHub Actions provides an easy and effective starting point.

train.content: how do you recover from developer burnout?

Burnout is physical and emotional exhaustion — very common in software. Symptoms: loss of motivation, constant fatigue, irritability, decreased productivity, feeling of 'what difference does it make.' Causes: excessive overtime, unclear requirements, constant context switching, lack of recognition, impostor syndrome. Short-term solutions: take time off (truly disconnect), physical activity, fix your sleep schedule, focus on small completable tasks. Long-term: set boundaries (no after-hours work), learn to say 'no,' work on passion projects different from work, pick up a non-coding hobby, consider therapy or coaching. Sometimes an environment change is necessary — staying in a toxic workplace causes long-term damage. Burnout isn't weakness, it's the natural result of overloading. Early intervention matters — act before it becomes chronic.

train.content: what is Kubernetes and why use it?

Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestration platform that automatically manages containers. Running Docker containers is easy — but managing 100 containers across 10 servers, auto-restarting crashed ones, load balancing, and performing updates is hard. Kubernetes automates all of that. Key concepts: Pod (smallest unit, usually 1 container), Deployment (defines desired state of Pods), Service (provides network access to Pods), Ingress (routes external traffic). Self-healing: automatically restarts crashed containers. Auto-scaling: adds new pods when load increases. Rolling update: zero-downtime updates. It has a steep learning curve but is essential for large-scale applications. You can try it locally with Minikube.

train.content: what are ACID properties in databases?

ACID ensures database transaction reliability through 4 properties. Atomicity: a transaction either completes fully or not at all — in a money transfer, the debit without the credit can never happen. Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another — constraints are never violated. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't affect each other — isolation levels exist (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable). Durability: committed transactions are permanent even if the system crashes — ensured by WAL (Write-Ahead Logging). PostgreSQL is fully ACID compliant. MongoDB added multi-document ACID transaction support since version 4.0. ACID is essential for financial applications — that's why Gorkem's banking project uses SQL.

train.content: how do you prevent SQL injection?

SQL injection is one of the most dangerous and common vulnerabilities. An attacker injects SQL code into input: ' OR 1=1 -- for example. The result: the entire database can be read, deleted, or modified. Prevention: 1) Parameterized queries / Prepared statements — NEVER build SQL with string concatenation. Python: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s', (user_id,)). 2) Use an ORM (Django ORM, SQLAlchemy) — automatically parameterizes queries. 3) Input validation — reject inputs that don't match expected formats. 4) Least privilege — give database users minimum permissions, no DROP TABLE rights. 5) WAF (Web Application Firewall) for additional protection. 6) Regular security scanning (OWASP ZAP, SQLMap). Using parameterized queries in Gorkem's projects is a fundamental security practice.

train.content: should I choose MongoDB or PostgreSQL?

It depends on your project's needs. PostgreSQL is a relational database — ACID compliant, great for complex queries and JOINs, preferred for financial applications where consistency matters. MongoDB is a NoSQL document store — flexible schema, JSON-like documents, ideal for rapid prototyping and projects with frequently changing schemas. Performance comparison: PostgreSQL excels at complex queries, MongoDB has advantages in horizontal scaling and write-heavy workloads. For most web applications, either works. Choose PostgreSQL for e-commerce, banking, and consistency-critical apps; MongoDB for IoT, logging, CMS, and flexible schema needs. Gorkem's banking-management-system uses SQL because financial data consistency is critical.

train.content: what is database normalization?

Normalization is the process of reducing data redundancy and improving consistency in database design. 1NF: single value per cell, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependencies — all non-key columns fully depend on the primary key. 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependencies — if A determines B determines C, move C to a separate table. BCNF: stricter version of 3NF. 4NF and 5NF handle multi-valued and join dependencies, rarely needed in practice. Most applications work fine with 3NF. Be careful: over-normalization can hurt performance — sometimes intentional denormalization is needed, especially in read-heavy systems. Data warehouses prefer denormalized structures like star schemas.
what are database indexing strategies?

Indexes dramatically speed up database queries — think of it like a book's index. B-Tree index is the most common: ideal for equality and range queries. Hash index: only for equality queries, very fast. Composite index: single index on multiple columns — perfect for WHERE a=1 AND b=2 queries. Partial index: indexes only rows matching a condition — like WHERE status='active'. Covering index: includes all columns the query needs, answering without touching the table. Warning: every index slows down writes and uses disk space. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to examine query plans and remove unnecessary indexes. Good rule: add indexes on columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY but don't overdo it.

train.content: how do you negotiate salary as a developer?

Salary negotiation is a skill most developers avoid but it's very important. Preparation: research the market (Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, LinkedIn Salary), know your worth, determine your minimum acceptable number. Don't give the first number — respond to 'what are your expectations?' with 'I'm expecting a competitive offer based on market rates' or give a range. When you receive an offer, don't accept immediately — say 'I need to think about it' and wait at least 24-48 hours. When making a counter-offer, provide justification: market data, your experience, projects, value you'll bring. Negotiate more than salary — remote work, flexible hours, education budget, stock options, vacation days are all negotiable. Negotiating doesn't show weakness, it shows professionalism. Worst case, they say no and the original offer still stands.

train.content: what does the CAP theorem say?

CAP theorem states that distributed systems can provide at most 2 out of 3 properties simultaneously. Consistency: every read returns the most recent data. Availability: every request gets a response, even during failures. Partition Tolerance: the system keeps working despite network splits. In practice, partition tolerance is mandatory since networks aren't always reliable, so the choice is between CP or AP. CP systems (MongoDB, HBase): choose consistency — some requests are rejected during partitions. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB): choose availability — temporarily stale data may be returned (eventual consistency). In reality, it's not completely black and white — the PACELC theorem provides a more detailed model. Understanding this trade-off is critical in system design.

train.content: what is clean architecture?

Clean Architecture is Robert C. Martin's (Uncle Bob) architectural approach. The core idea: business logic should be independent from the outside world — if the framework, database, or UI changes, the core domain shouldn't change. Layers (inside out): Entities (business rules), Use Cases (application logic), Interface Adapters (controllers, presenters, gateways), Frameworks & Drivers (web framework, DB, UI). The Dependency Rule: dependencies always point inward — inner layers don't know about outer ones. Benefits: testability (test business logic without a database), flexibility (switch from PostgreSQL to MongoDB without changing core), understandability. Drawbacks: overly complex for small projects, lots of boilerplate code. Valuable for large, long-lived projects — but may be overengineering for a startup MVP.

train.content: what is domain-driven design DDD?

DDD is Eric Evans' approach for modeling complex business logic. Core idea: software structure should mirror the business domain's structure. Ubiquitous Language: developers and domain experts speak the same language — use it in code too. Bounded Context: divide the large system into independent regions — the same term can mean different things in different contexts (Customer in orders vs CRM). Entity: objects with identity (User, Order). Value Object: identity-less, defined by its value (Address, Money). Aggregate: consistency boundary — group of entities that must change together. Repository: provides access to aggregates. Domain Event: events like 'order created.' DDD is very valuable for projects with complex business logic but unnecessary for simple CRUD applications.
